lessons.title: Observe
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 2–4 · Activity Book pp. 1–2
lessons.objective: Record three relevant observations and name the sense used for each.
lessons.materials: A fabric swatch, a wooden block, a closed shaker, pencils and a three-row observation table.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils recorded three valid pairs. Follow up with a guided property-and-sense match.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a swatch and a block. Ask which properties pupils can identify using sight or touch.
Describe one visible property and one property they can feel.
Main activity · 30 min
Model one observation using “I notice … using …”. Guide pairs through three stations for sight, touch and hearing.
At each station, observe one item, record its property and name the sense used. Compare entries with a partner.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Check three entries per pupil for a property and a matching sense. Give prompts where an entry is a guess.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 1–2 if available. Independently submit three property-and-sense pairs.
Closure · 5 min
Ask pupils to give one observation that another person could check.
Share a property and name how they checked it.

lessons.title: Classify
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 5–7 · Activity Book pp. 3–4
lessons.objective: Sort six pictures into two groups using one observable feature and state the rule used.
lessons.materials: Animal picture cards and two sorting mats per pair. Use clear full-body pictures.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils sorted all six cards and stated a consistent rule. Revisit one observable feature with pupils who changed rules halfway.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a duck and a goat. Ask pupils to identify a feature visible in one picture only.
Point to a feature and describe the difference.
Main activity · 30 min
Model how one feature produces two groups. Give pairs six cards and ask them to check each card against their rule.
Sort the cards, label each group and explain one decision to a partner. Test a second feature if time permits.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give pictures of a chicken, an owl, a parrot, a cat, a horse and a rabbit. Check that the labels express opposite outcomes of one visible feature and all six placements follow the rule.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 3–4 if available. Individually sort the new pictures, then write or say the rule.
Closure · 5 min
Move one card to the wrong group and ask for a correction.
Move the card back and justify the placement using the feature.

lessons.title: Measure and Use Numbers
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 8–10 · Activity Book pp. 5–6
lessons.objective: Measure two straight paper strips to the nearest centimetre and record both readings with the correct unit.
lessons.materials: 30 cm rulers, pre-cut strips in whole-centimetre lengths and a two-row recording table.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils recorded both measurements with the correct unit. Reteach zero alignment using a marked start line where needed.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show two strips with different starting positions. Ask how to compare their lengths fairly.
Suggest lining up the ends and using the same ruler.
Main activity · 30 min
Demonstrate aligning an end to the zero mark and reading the other end from above. Deliberately start at the 1 cm mark and ask pupils to identify the error.
Take turns measuring and checking with a partner. Record each length in a table with the unit cm.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give each pupil two unmarked strips of 8 cm and 14 cm. Check ruler placement and both readings.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 5–6 if available. Independently measure the two strips and label both readings with cm.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what information is missing if a measurement is written as “12”.
Give the unit and explain where to place the strip to start.

lessons.title: Communicate
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 10–11 · Activity Book pp. 7–8
lessons.objective: Present two accurate findings from a tally using a labelled table and one spoken or written comparison.
lessons.materials: Bags of coloured counters, tally sheets and pencils.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils reported two accurate totals and a correct comparison. Revisit the use of headings and reading across a row.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show an unlabelled tally. Ask what a reader needs to know to interpret it.
Suggest labels for what was counted and the number counted.
Main activity · 30 min
Give groups counters in three colours. Model the first table row and ask how the row helps a listener understand the findings.
Count the counters, agree on totals and take turns explaining a finding using their table.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give each pupil a new tally showing four red, six blue and two yellow counters. Check the headings, the red and blue totals, and the comparison.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 7–8 if available. Convert the tally into a labelled table independently, then report the red and blue totals and say which colour has more.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what would make a classmate's table easy to understand.
Identify one useful feature, such as clear category headings.

lessons.title: Use Apparatus and Handle Specimens
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 12–14 · Activity Book pp. 9–10 (shared section reference)
lessons.objective: Independently use a dropper to wet cotton wool without pooling water and place two seeds gently with blunt tweezers.
lessons.materials: Water, plastic droppers, shallow clear cups, cotton wool, dried beans, blunt tweezers and trays. Tell pupils the beans are for observation.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils met all three checks. Give pupils who squeezed too much water a short dropper practice task.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show two prepared cups, one with damp cotton wool and one with pooled water. Ask which tool helps control the amount.
Choose a dropper and describe the difference between the cups.
Main activity · 30 min
Demonstrate drawing water into the dropper and adding it a few drops at a time. Show how to lift a bean gently over the tray.
Take turns preparing a cup. Stop when the cotton wool is evenly damp and place two beans apart so both can be seen.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give each pupil a clean setup and check dropper use, absence of pooled water, and careful transfer of both seeds.
Independently prepare one cup, then explain how the dropper or tweezers helped. Refer to the relevant items in Activity Book pp. 9–10 if available.
Closure · 5 min
Ask how to correct a setup with too much water.
Explain how adding a few drops at a time prevents pooling.

lessons.title: Sketch and Clean Apparatus
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 12–14 · Activity Book pp. 9–10 (shared section reference)
lessons.objective: Make a recognisable sketch with three correct labels and clean the plastic cup and dropper without leaving visible residue.
lessons.materials: A clear plastic cup with a bean and damp cotton wool, plastic dropper, shallow tray, clean rinse water and a draining rack. Prepare a second cup and dropper used with water and a pinch of sugar for cleaning practice.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils completed the sketch and cleaning checks. Reteach the sketch or rinsing step that each pupil missed.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a simple line drawing of a cup and ask what would make the specimen inside easy to identify.
Suggest showing the bean outline and adding a clear label.
Main activity · 30 min
Model drawing from the side, then show how to rinse a used cup and draw and expel clean water through the dropper over the tray.
Practise sketching the cup setup with a partner. Take turns rinsing the used cup and dropper and placing them on the rack.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Check each pupil's sketch for a clear outline and correct labels for the cup, bean and cotton wool. Observe each pupil rinsing both items and checking for residue.
Sketch and label the setup independently. Clean the used cup and dropper, then show both items to the teacher.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why a dropper used for sugar solution still needs rinsing if the liquid looks clear.
Explain that clear liquid can still contain dissolved sugar, then describe how to rinse the dropper.

lessons.title: Store Apparatus and Substances
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 12–14 · Activity Book pp. 9–10 (shared section reference)
lessons.objective: Return three items to their designated places and explain what to do with a wet cup before storage.
lessons.materials: A clean dry plastic cup, a clean dry plastic dropper, a closed labelled container of table sugar, a wet cup, an equipment tray, a substance shelf and a drying rack.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils stored all three items correctly and identified the drying step. Repeat the routine with pupils who mixed equipment and substances.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a wet cup beside a dry cup. Ask which is ready to put away.
Choose the dry cup and give one reason.
Main activity · 30 min
Model checking that apparatus is clean and dry and that the substance lid is closed. Point out the storage labels and drying rack.
In pairs, check sample items, choose the correct location and explain why a wet item goes to the rack.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Observe each pupil returning a dry cup, a dry dropper and the closed sugar container. Check all three locations and the response to the wet cup.
Put the three items away independently. Point to the drying rack and explain when the wet cup can be stored.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what to check before returning the sugar container.
Check the label and confirm that the lid is closed.

lessons.title: Follow Science Room Rules
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 18–20 · Activity Book pp. 11–12
lessons.objective: Follow the agreed entry, incident-reporting and clean-up routines during a practical activity, and explain how one rule prevents harm.
lessons.materials: Plastic cups, plastic spoons, water, trays, cleaning cloths, incident picture cards and a pupil checklist. Use a picture to simulate a spill or damaged item.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils followed all three routines independently and explained one safety reason. Practise the missed routine with pupils who needed a prompt before the next practical activity.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Mark the bag area and show how to keep the walkway clear. Record each pupil's entry action on the checklist.
Leave bags in the agreed area, walk to the assigned station and wait for instructions.
Main activity · 30 min
Demonstrate transferring a spoonful of water between cups over a tray. Show an incident card to one group at a time and observe how each pupil reports it.
Take turns moving water over the tray. When shown an incident card, stop, leave the affected item alone and tell the teacher where it is and what happened.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Observe each pupil clean and return one item. Use three checklist columns for entry, reporting and clean-up. Recheck an action after a short prompt where needed.
Clean and return assigned equipment independently. Explain to the teacher or write how a clear walkway or immediate reporting keeps people safe.
Closure · 5 min
Review the response to a damaged item and ask which action to take first.
State the first action. Use Activity Book pp. 11–12 for follow-up if available.

lessons.title: Human Reproduction
lessons.references: Textbook p. 24 · Activity Book p. 13
lessons.objective: State that humans reproduce by giving birth and select the picture that shows a new human entering a family.
lessons.materials: Teacher-made cards showing a newborn with a caregiver, an older child, and an unrelated picture of an egg hatching.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils selected the correct picture and stated how humans reproduce. Revisit the vocabulary using the newborn card.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a picture of a newborn with a caregiver. Ask which person has just been born.
Point to the newborn and describe what they see.
Main activity · 30 min
Introduce the words human, newborn and giving birth. Compare the two human cards and ask which represents the arrival of a new baby.
Sort the pictures, match the newborn card to the phrase “giving birth” and say how humans reproduce.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Show three new drawings: a newborn with a caregiver, a child reading and a chick hatching. Ask “Which drawing shows a human who has just been born?” and “How do humans reproduce?”
Independently select the newborn picture and answer the second question in a sentence.
Closure · 5 min
Ask for the key sentence again and connect it to the next lesson on changes after birth.
State that humans reproduce by giving birth.

lessons.title: Describe Growth Since Birth
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 25–27 · Activity Book pp. 14–15
lessons.objective: Use the records for one fictional child to describe the changes in body size, height and weight between birth and age seven.
lessons.materials: Stage cards and a fictional record showing 50 cm and 3 kg at birth and 120 cm and 23 kg at age seven, with two illustrations of the same child.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils described all three changes and cited one pair of readings. Revisit the units with pupils who confused height and weight.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show the child's two pictures. Ask how the earlier and later stages differ.
Identify the baby and the older child and name one visible change.
Main activity · 30 min
Model reading a two-row growth record. Ask which column shows height and which shows weight. Use pictures to discuss body size.
Put the stage cards in order and use the record and pictures to make one statement about each change.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give a new fictional example, with 49 cm and 3 kg at birth and 117 cm and 21 kg at age seven. Check all three statements against the pictures and record.
Independently describe the changes in body size, height and weight. Cite one pair of readings as evidence.
Closure · 5 min
Ask how to distinguish what was seen in the picture from what was read in the record.
Identify the evidence used for body size and for one measured change.

lessons.title: Compare Growth Among Individuals
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 28–30 · Activity Book p. 16
lessons.objective: Compare two sets of measurements for fictional children of the same age and use at least two findings to conclude that individuals can grow differently.
lessons.materials: Teacher-made paper hand outlines with pre-checked lengths, rulers and anonymised model records. Do not collect pupils' own body measurements.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils used two accurate findings to support the conclusion. Repeat one comparison using a side-by-side table where needed.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show two different hand outlines labelled “Age 7”. Ask whether equal age means equal size.
Suggest a measurement that could test the idea.
Main activity · 30 min
Model measuring hand length from a marked wrist line to the longest fingertip. Give pairs two outlines and the matching fictional height records.
Measure both outlines, record the lengths and compare them alongside the heights. Discuss why one measurement cannot describe all growth.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give a fresh pair of outlines measuring 12 cm and 14 cm, with heights of 123 cm and 118 cm. Check two accurate comparisons and an evidence-based conclusion.
Independently measure the outlines and write one comparison about hand length, one about height and one conclusion.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what the examples show about children of the same age.
Explain that their measurements can differ and point to one result.

lessons.title: Recognise Inherited Features
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 30–32 · Activity Book pp. 17–20 (shared section reference)
lessons.objective: Explain that features can be inherited from parents or earlier generations and identify two possible inherited features in a fictional family chart.
lessons.materials: Illustrated fictional family charts and feature cards for iris colour, hair type and skin colour.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils identified two examples and explained inheritance. Revisit feature categories with a labelled picture.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show two fictional relatives with the same hair type. Ask pupils to describe the feature.
Describe the shared hair type using the illustration.
Main activity · 30 min
Model reading a fictional family chart across two generations. Explain that a shared feature may be inherited and that a picture alone cannot tell which relative it came from.
Circle two shared features and discuss why clothing or a hairstyle chosen for the day is a different kind of similarity.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give a fictional chart showing that Aina and her mother have brown irises, and Aina and her grandfather have wavy hair. Check both examples and the explanation.
Independently name two possible inherited features, identify the people who share them and explain the idea in one sentence.
Closure · 5 min
Ask for one feature pupils can compare on a chart.
Name a feature and point to an example in the fictional chart.

lessons.title: Communicate Findings About Growth and Heredity
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 33–34 · Activity Book pp. 19–20
lessons.objective: Communicate one growth observation and one possible inherited feature, giving relevant evidence for both from a fictional case.
lessons.materials: Case cards with two dated height readings and a fictional family illustration, pencils and a two-box response sheet.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils gave both findings with supporting evidence. Provide the sentence stem “I know this because …” for the missing explanation.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a height record and a fictional family chart. Ask which source answers a question about change over time.
Choose the height record and explain why it has two readings.
Main activity · 30 min
Model a growth statement supported by two readings and an inheritance statement supported by a shared feature. Offer a labelled sketch or short oral report.
Prepare a two-part explanation with a partner and check that the evidence matches each statement.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give a new case with heights of 104 cm and 121 cm and a chart showing shared curly hair. Check one supported finding of each type.
Independently present both findings through a labelled sketch, two short written statements or an oral explanation.
Closure · 5 min
Ask pupils to name the evidence that makes one of their statements clear.
Point to the two readings or the shared feature in the chart.

lessons.title: How Animals Reproduce
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 36–37 · Activity Book pp. 21–22 (shared section reference)
lessons.objective: State the two ways animals reproduce shown in the textbook and give one correct example of each.
lessons.materials: Picture pairs showing a duck with eggs and a goat with its young, plus picture cards of a crocodile nest and an elephant calf.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils stated both ways and gave a correct example for each. Repeat the picture-to-phrase match where needed.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a duckling and a kid. Ask how each came into the world.
Make a prediction for each animal.
Main activity · 30 min
Reveal the picture evidence and model the phrases “lays eggs” and “gives birth to live young”. Introduce the crocodile and elephant cards and ask which phrase fits each.
Match a phrase to each picture pair and explain their choices to a partner.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Hand out an exit slip showing a duck and an elephant with their young. Ask pupils to state the two ways and label each example.
Independently write or say “lays eggs” and “gives birth to live young”, then match them to the duck and elephant.
Closure · 5 min
Ask for one example of each way and point to the matching pictures.
State the two examples in full sentences.

lessons.title: Classify Animals by Reproduction
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 36–38 · Activity Book pp. 21–22 (shared section reference)
lessons.objective: Classify at least five of six animals by their way of reproducing and justify one choice using a clue.
lessons.materials: Two-column sorting mat and illustrated clues for duck, crocodile, mosquito, goat, bat and elephant.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils placed at least five animals correctly and justified one choice. Revisit the evidence on any misplaced card.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Hold up a bat and a duck card. Ask what evidence would tell us how each reproduces.
Suggest looking for eggs or evidence of a live birth.
Main activity · 30 min
Model sorting a duck using a picture of its nest. Give teams the clue cards and ask them to read the evidence before they place each animal.
Sort the cards, then swap one example with another team and explain its placement.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give each pupil a shuffled six-card sheet with short clues. Check for at least five correct placements and one justification.
Independently place the animals in the two groups and explain one choice using its clue.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why a duck and a bat can both fly and still belong in different groups.
Identify the way each reproduces as the sorting rule.

lessons.title: Animals That Lay Few or Many Eggs
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 39–40 · Activity Book p. 23
lessons.objective: Use two observation pictures to explain one example of an animal that lays few eggs and one that lays many eggs.
lessons.materials: Swan nest and frogspawn illustrations, counters for the swan nest, and an illustrated observation sheet with a swan and a fish example.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils explained both examples with picture evidence. Revisit the few-versus-many comparison with counters.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Display a swan nest and a frogspawn picture side by side. Ask which has more visible eggs.
Point to the picture with more eggs and describe the clue.
Main activity · 30 min
Use counters to represent the eggs in the illustrated swan nest. Show a large cluster of frog eggs and ask pupils to compare the observations.
Make a sketch of each observation and describe which animal laid few eggs and which laid many in the examples.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give pupils a swan-nest illustration and a fish-egg cluster with the animal named. Check one evidence-based sentence for each picture.
Independently name the animals, use “few” or “many” for each and refer to the eggs shown.
Closure · 5 min
Ask for one pair of examples from the lesson.
Compare the swan and frog examples in one sentence.

lessons.title: Animals That Give Birth to Few or Many Young
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 41–42 · Activity Book p. 24
lessons.objective: Give one example each of an animal that gives birth to few and many young, supported by the number shown in an illustrated birth record.
lessons.materials: Model birth records for an elephant with one calf, a rabbit with six kits, a dolphin with one calf and a cat with five kittens.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils gave both examples and supported them with the counts shown. Repeat the comparison using counters if needed.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show an elephant birth record and ask how many young were born in that record.
Count the calf and state the number.
Main activity · 30 min
Compare the elephant record with the rabbit record. Ask what the two examples show about the number born at a time.
Fill a two-row table with animal, number born and “few” or “many”. Explain the comparison to a partner.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give the dolphin and cat records. Ask pupils to compare them and check the names and evidence.
Independently write or say that the dolphin is the “few” example and the cat is the “many” example, citing the two counts.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what pupils looked at to decide between “few” and “many”.
State that they compared how many young were born in the examples.

lessons.title: Record Changes During Animal Growth
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 45–46 · Activity Book pp. 25–27
lessons.objective: Sequence four illustrated frog life-cycle stages and record two observable changes between stages.
lessons.materials: Frog and cow life-cycle illustrations, four shuffled frog cards and a recording strip.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils ordered four stages and recorded two supported changes. Revisit the pair of stages pupils confused.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a tadpole and an adult frog. Ask pupils to point to one visible difference.
Describe a feature such as the tail or legs.
Main activity · 30 min
Model how to record the appearance of a stage from an illustration. Use calf and adult cow illustrations to practise recording an observation, then distribute the frog cards.
Sequence frog eggs, tadpole, froglet and adult frog. Discuss the froglet’s legs and the shorter tail, then compare the froglet with the adult frog.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Hand out a fresh four-image frog strip in a different order. Check the sequence and two changes between neighbouring stages.
Independently number the stages and record two changes using arrows, labelled sketches or short phrases.
Closure · 5 min
Ask which pair of images supports one change.
Point to two stages and read out the change.

lessons.title: Compare Young Animals and Their Adults
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 43–44 · Activity Book p. 28
lessons.objective: Compare two young-and-adult pairs and support each comparison with a visible feature.
lessons.materials: Paired pictures of a kitten and adult cat, a calf and adult cow, a caterpillar and adult butterfly, and a tadpole and adult frog.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils made two accurate comparisons with visible features. Revisit the comparison using labelled pictures.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show the kitten and adult cat. Ask which features can be seen on both.
Identify a shared feature such as four legs.
Main activity · 30 min
Model using the same feature to compare both pictures. Contrast the adult butterfly's wings with the caterpillar picture.
Match young animals to their adults and mark a visible similarity or difference on each pair.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give pupils the cow and frog pairs. Check one comparison supported by a feature for each pair.
Independently explain how the calf resembles the cow and how the tadpole differs from the adult frog.
Closure · 5 min
Ask for one example of a young animal that looks noticeably different from its adult.
Name the example and point to the feature that supports it.

lessons.title: Communicate Observations About Reproduction and Growth
lessons.references: Textbook p. 46 and p. 48 · Teacher-made assessment
lessons.objective: Communicate one observation about reproduction and two about growth using evidence from one illustrated life cycle.
lessons.materials: Butterfly life-cycle pictures showing an adult laying eggs, a caterpillar, a chrysalis and an adult butterfly, plus paper for labelled sketches.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils communicated all three observations with picture evidence. Offer a three-box prompt for the missing observation.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a butterfly laying eggs and ask pupils which detail tells us how it reproduces.
Point to the eggs and describe what the adult does.
Main activity · 30 min
Demonstrate how to mark the reproduction observation separately from changes in growth on a simple picture sequence. Give pairs a set of cycle pictures.
Rehearse a short report with a partner. Point to the egg-laying image and explain two changes shown across the pictures.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Invite each pupil to make a labelled sketch, write a short report or give an oral account. Check the reproduction observation and two growth observations against the pictures.
Independently communicate that the adult lays eggs, that a caterpillar hatches and that an adult with wings emerges from the chrysalis, or give other supported observations.
Closure · 5 min
Invite one pupil to share an observation and show its evidence.
Listen and locate the matching picture.

lessons.title: Explain Why Plants Are Important
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 49–50 · Activity Book p. 29
lessons.objective: Give one example of how a plant helps people and one of how a plant helps an animal, with the benefit named in each example.
lessons.materials: Pictures of rice, a mango tree, a bird nest in a tree and a caterpillar feeding on leaves; two-column recording slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils named both recipients and their benefits correctly. Revisit the picture clues with pupils who named a plant without a benefit.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a rice plant beside a bowl of rice and ask how the pictures are connected.
Describe the link between the plant and the food.
Main activity · 30 min
Model a benefit statement using the rice pictures. Give pairs pictures of the tree, nest and feeding caterpillar and ask what each animal gets from a plant.
Sort the examples into food and shelter, then explain a picture using “The plant provides … for …”.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Show a mango fruit eaten by a person and a bird sheltering in a tree. Check one correct benefit for each recipient.
Independently write or say that the mango tree provides food for a person and that the tree provides shelter for the bird.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what the caterpillar gets from the plant and how pupils can tell.
Name food as the benefit and point to the feeding evidence.

lessons.title: Identify What Seeds Need to Germinate
lessons.references: Textbook p. 51 · Activity Book pp. 30–31
lessons.objective: State the three conditions needed for seed germination and identify the missing condition in two illustrated examples.
lessons.materials: Dry and germinated mung beans; teacher-made condition cards showing moist cotton at room temperature, dry cotton, reduced access to air and a cold location.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils identified both missing conditions and stated all three needs. Review the condition cards with pupils who confuse a seed's needs with those of a growing plant.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Compare a dry seed with a germinated seed. Ask what visible change tells us germination has started.
Point to the root emerging from the seed and describe the change.
Main activity · 30 min
Introduce water, air and a suitable temperature. Show a reference condition and compare one changed condition at a time using the cards.
Match condition cards to water, air or temperature. Predict which condition is suitable and explain why.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give each pupil a dry-cotton case and a cold-location case with the other conditions stated. Ask pupils to identify each missing condition and list all three needs.
Independently identify water and a suitable temperature in the respective cases, then state all three germination needs.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what “suitable temperature” means for the seed shown.
Explain that the seed needs a temperature at which it can germinate.

lessons.title: Record Changes From Seed to Seedling
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 52–53 · Activity Book p. 32
lessons.objective: Record the height and number of visible leaves at three observed stages of mung-bean growth and describe two changes using the records.
lessons.materials: Living mung-bean specimens prepared in advance at three stages, labels showing days since sowing, rulers and individual observation tables.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils completed the three records and described two supported changes. Repeat the measurement or counting method where results were inconsistent.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a newly germinated seed and an older seedling. Ask what could be measured or counted.
Suggest comparing the height or counting visible leaves.
Main activity · 30 min
Demonstrate measuring each specimen from its support surface to the shoot tip and agree which visible leaves to count. Guide groups to visit the labelled specimens in order.
Observe the real seeds and seedlings, measure and count using the same method, then compare observations within the group.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask each pupil to complete a three-row table and describe two changes supported by their own observations. Check the units and the match between each conclusion and its data.
Record the day, height in centimetres and leaf count, then compare two stages using the recorded values.
Closure · 5 min
Invite a pupil to point to the values that support one observed change.
Read out the values and describe the change.

lessons.title: Sequence the Stages of Plant Growth
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 54–55 · Activity Book pp. 33–34
lessons.objective: Arrange five stages of a flowering plant's growth and explain one visible change between adjacent stages.
lessons.materials: Labelled tomato sequence for modelling, shuffled okra stage cards and a five-box recording strip.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils ordered all five stages and explained a change. Revisit any swapped stages using the visual clue on each card.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a flower and a fruit from the same kind of plant. Ask which appeared first.
Predict the order and give a reason.
Main activity · 30 min
Model using a visible clue to place a germinating seed after a seed. Give groups the tomato cards and ask them to check each pair of neighbouring stages.
Arrange seed, germination, young plant, flowering and fruiting. Point to a clue that distinguishes each neighbouring pair.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give each pupil shuffled okra pictures. Check the five positions and one explanation that uses picture evidence.
Independently order and label the pictures, then explain a change such as flowers appearing after the young plant stage.
Closure · 5 min
Ask which picture shows that the seed has started to grow.
Identify the germination picture and point to the emerging root.

lessons.title: Investigate What Plants Need to Grow
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 56–58 · Activity Book p. 35
lessons.objective: Compare two plants in a fair watering investigation and use a recorded observation to explain why water matters, then name air and sunlight as further needs and nutrients as supporting growth.
lessons.materials: Two similar seedlings in identical pots, dated class observations from a seven-day investigation, labels, a measuring cup and a comparison sheet.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils drew the water conclusion from evidence and identified the other requirements. Compare the original records again where pupils give a prediction as an observation.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show the two plants and ask which differences pupils can observe.
Describe the leaves or stem of each plant.
Main activity · 30 min

Review the class investigation. Both pots received the same light and growing medium, with watering as the changed condition. Ask pupils to compare the first- and seventh-day records. Use the textbook results to discuss air, sunlight and the role of nutrients.
Compare the live plants and the records, identify what changed and what was kept the same, then point to evidence for the effect of watering.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask each pupil to complete one evidence sentence about water and label a plant diagram with its further needs and the role of nutrients.
Independently describe a recorded difference, link it to watering, name air and sunlight, and explain that nutrients help plants grow.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why both pots were kept in the same place.
Explain that the comparison used the same light for both plants.

lessons.title: Explain Observations About a Plant's Life
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 57–59 · Activity Book p. 36
lessons.objective: Explain two observations from a plant record and use them to predict one effect of interrupted growth on a person or an animal.
lessons.materials: Dated class sketches or photos of a seed and seedling, pictures of a healthy and a wilted plant, and a three-box storyboard.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils explained two supported observations and gave a plausible prediction. Use the storyboard to revisit any missing link.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show two dated plant observations and ask which changes can be seen.
Identify a visible change between the records.
Main activity · 30 min
Model how to connect an observation to an explanation. Compare conditions for germination with those for later growth and discuss an example of a plant used for food.
In pairs, rehearse a short explanation using two dated records and predict what could happen if plants stop growing before they produce food.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask pupils to explain two observations and one consequence using a labelled sketch, short writing or an oral explanation. Check the distinction between observations and prediction.
Independently explain two visible changes using the records and predict a consequence, such as fewer leaves available for a leaf-eating animal.
Closure · 5 min
Ask which statement came directly from the observation and which described a possible future outcome.
Identify one observation and the prediction based on it.

lessons.title: Identify Sources of Light
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 61–63 · Activity Book p. 37
lessons.objective: Identify three sources of light and explain why a mirror in the same scene is a reflector.
lessons.materials: Pictures of the Sun and a lit candle, a battery torch, mirror, white card and four illustrated response prompts.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils identified all three sources and explained the role of the mirror. Repeat the torch and mirror demonstration with pupils who confused reflection with emission.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a battery torch switched off and on. Ask when it gives light.
Compare the two states and identify the lit torch as a source.
Main activity · 30 min
Use the torch and mirror to make a patch of light on a card. Switch the torch off and ask what changes. Give pairs scene cards to sort.
Observe that the patch disappears. Sort the Sun, a lit candle, a lit torch and a mirror by whether each gives out its own light.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Show a new illustration with the Sun, a glowing lamp, a candle flame and a mirror. Check all three choices and the explanation about the mirror.
Independently mark the three sources and explain that the mirror sends light from another source towards the viewer.
Closure · 5 min
Ask which of the three sources can light an outdoor playground during the day.
Identify the Sun and describe one sign that its light reaches the playground.

lessons.title: Compare Activities in Light and Dark
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 64–65 · Activity Book pp. 38–40
lessons.objective: Compare success at identifying symbols in light and dark and give one conclusion supported by the recorded observations.
lessons.materials: Identical enclosed viewing boxes with the same arrangement of four large symbols, torch mounted on one box, second symbol set, recording slips and a picture of a reader.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils compared both observations and explained the effect of light. Practise turning paired results into a comparison sentence with pupils who gave only one result.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a picture of someone trying to read a sign when a light is off. Ask pupils what would help.
Suggest turning on a light and predict how it will affect reading.
Main activity · 30 min

Use a lit and an unlit box while the classroom remains lit. Give the same viewing time and symbol positions in both conditions. Rotate which box is viewed first and use a second equivalent symbol set to reduce recall.
Count how many symbols they can identify correctly in each condition and record both observations. Compare their results with a partner.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give a sample result of four correct in the lit box and one in the unlit box. Ask each pupil to interpret the evidence and apply it to reading the sign.
Independently identify the easier condition, cite both results and explain why the sign is easier to read when lit.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why both viewing times should match.
Explain that keeping the time the same makes the comparison about the light.

lessons.title: Explain How a Shadow Forms
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 66–67 · Activity Book p. 41
lessons.objective: Make a shadow on a screen and identify the correct arrangement in two contrasting diagrams, explaining how the shadow forms.
lessons.materials: LED torch, card silhouette with a stand, white card screen, marked mat and individual diagram slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils located the shadow and explained that light was blocked. Rebuild the arrangement with pupils who placed the shadow on the torch side of the card.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Shine a torch onto a screen and ask where to place a card to darken part of the screen.
Predict a position for the card and explain their choice.
Main activity · 30 min
Keep the screen and torch fixed. Ask pairs to put the card between them, then off to one side. Keep the torch aimed at the screen.
Test both positions, draw the arrangement and record whether a shadow appears on the screen.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give diagrams with the card in the beam and to the side. Ask pupils to mark the shadow position and explain it.
Independently identify the in-beam arrangement, shade the region behind the card on the screen and explain that the card blocks light.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what happens to the shadow when the card is removed.
Predict that the patch disappears as light reaches the screen again.

lessons.title: Investigate the Clarity of Shadows
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 67–68 · Activity Book p. 42
lessons.objective: Record the shadow clarity of three materials in a fair comparison and support a conclusion with at least two observations.
lessons.materials: Same-sized shapes cut from card, tracing paper and clear acetate, clips, LED torch, white screen and marked positions.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils recorded three observations and used two in their explanation. Repeat the comparison for pupils who changed the torch or object position during trials.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Hold a card shape and an acetate shape of the same size against the same light. Ask what might appear on the screen.
Predict which material will make a clearer shadow and give a reason.
Main activity · 30 min
Mark the positions for the torch, material and screen. Use the same lighting and orientation for all three trials. Model recording clear, less clear or no discernible shadow.
Take turns changing only the material. Observe the screen, record results for all three and compare the sharpness or visibility of the shadows.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask for an individual record and a comparison sentence naming two materials and their observed outcomes. Accept faint edges on clear acetate when reported accurately.
Independently name the clearest shadow, compare it with another trial and explain the difference in terms of how much light passed through.
Closure · 5 min
Ask which material would best make a clearly visible shadow puppet.
Choose a material based on the recorded result.

lessons.title: Create a Shadow Game
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 69–71 · Activity Book pp. 43–44
lessons.objective: Create and demonstrate a guessing game with two distinct shadows and explain one change that made a shadow easier to recognise.
lessons.materials: LED torches, white screens, opaque card, blunt craft sticks, clips, two sample silhouette cards and an individual game slip.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils demonstrated two shadows and explained an improvement. Support pupils who need a clearer silhouette by testing it at a fixed position before changing the design.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show the shadow of a card bird behind a screen. Ask what clues make it recognisable.
Name a feature such as the beak or wings.
Main activity · 30 min
Demonstrate fixing a light and placing a silhouette between the light and the screen. Give pairs time to design two silhouettes, test them and refine a weak outline.
Make two different shapes. Show them in turn to a partner and revise the outline or angle if the partner cannot recognise the subject.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Watch each pupil operate the game and show two distinct shadows. Ask the pupil to describe one change made after the trial.
Independently run both clues, then draw or state the change and how it helped someone recognise a shape.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why card silhouettes usually work well for this game.
Link the visible outline to the card blocking light.

lessons.title: Explain Observations About Light and Dark
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 69, 71–72 · Activity Book pp. 43–44 (review of earlier trials)
lessons.objective: Communicate two observations about light and dark and explain each using a labelled sketch, written caption or oral response.
lessons.materials: Two class observation records from the viewing-box and shadow trials, example sketch with arrows and individual response cards.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils communicated two accurate observations with explanations. Revisit the relevant trial with pupils whose responses reported an outcome without its cause.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a photograph of a shadow from the previous lesson and ask what it shows and what caused it.
Give one observation and then a separate explanation.
Main activity · 30 min
Revisit the lighted and dark viewing boxes and a screen with an opaque shape in the beam. Model a short explanation backed by a visible result.
Compare the two demonstrations and discuss which observation supports each explanation. Practise labelling the source, object and shadow.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask each pupil to explain why symbols were easier to identify in the lit box and how the shadow appeared on the screen. Check each response against the observed evidence.
Independently present two observation–explanation pairs in their chosen format. Refer to the light in the viewing box and the blocked beam in the shadow trial.
Closure · 5 min
Invite a pupil to share one label or word that made the explanation clearer.
Share it and identify the observation it explains.

lessons.title: Identify Electrical Components
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 73–75 · Activity Book pp. 45–46
lessons.objective: Identify a dry cell, bulb and switch in a classroom kit and label all three on a picture of a circuit.
lessons.materials: Dry cell in a holder, miniature bulb in a holder, switch, connecting wires and circuit pictures.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils identified and labelled all three components. Revisit the physical components with pupils who labelled the holders.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a battery-powered lamp and ask which parts might be inside.
Suggest parts and compare them with the classroom kit.
Main activity · 30 min
Place the three components, holders and wires on a tray. Model distinguishing the cell from its holder and the bulb from its holder.
Match each component to its name, then locate the same components in a picture with a different layout.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Hand out an unlabelled circuit picture. Check that each label points to the component itself.
Independently label the dry cell, bulb and switch. Point to the equivalent components on the tray.
Closure · 5 min
Hold up a switch and a wire. Ask which item is the switch.
Identify the switch and distinguish it from the wire.

lessons.title: Explain the Functions of Circuit Components
lessons.references: Textbook p. 76 · Activity Book p. 47
lessons.objective: Explain the functions of the dry cell, bulb, switch and wires in a complete circuit, with at least three correct explanations including the switch.
lessons.materials: Working low-voltage classroom circuit, function cards and individual response slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils explained at least three functions, including the switch. Use the working circuit to revisit any mistaken function.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Close and open the switch in a working circuit. Ask which component was moved.
Identify the switch and describe the change at the bulb.
Main activity · 30 min
Trace the complete path. Describe how the dry cell supplies electrical energy, the bulb gives light, the wires connect the parts and the switch completes or breaks the path.
Match functions to the kit components and explain to a partner how closing and opening the switch affects the path.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give each pupil a four-component picture. Ask what each part does and check the explanation of the switch.
Independently describe each function and state that opening the switch breaks the circuit.
Closure · 5 min
Point to a wire between two components and ask what it does.
Explain that it joins the components in the electrical path.

lessons.title: Build a Complete Electric Circuit
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 77–78 · Activity Book p. 48
lessons.objective: Assemble a working circuit using a dry cell, bulb, switch and connecting wires, and demonstrate both the open and closed switch states.
lessons.materials: Teacher-checked dry-cell circuit kits with matched miniature bulbs, insulated leads and switches.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils assembled a working circuit and demonstrated both states. Rebuild the path with pupils who omitted a required connection.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a partly assembled kit and ask what path the bulb needs.
Trace a possible path from one dry-cell terminal to the other.
Main activity · 30 min
Model assembly with the switch open. Check that the path includes the bulb before pupils close the switch. Use the classroom dry-cell kits only.
Assemble the circuit in pairs. Trace the path through the bulb and switch, then observe the bulb with the switch closed and open.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give each pupil a turn to assemble and demonstrate the circuit. Check each required part and both observed states.
Independently connect the kit, show the bulb lighting with the switch closed and show it going out when the switch opens.
Closure · 5 min
Ask pupils to point out where the path is broken when the bulb goes out.
Point to the gap at the switch and leave the kit switched off.

lessons.title: Predict Why a Bulb Does Not Light
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 79–81 · Activity Book pp. 49–50
lessons.objective: Predict a likely cause for a bulb failing to light in two circuits and propose a check that tests each prediction.
lessons.materials: Known-good dry-cell kit, two teacher-prepared faulty setups with an open switch or loose lead, and a picture of a loose bulb.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils predicted both faults and proposed relevant checks. Revisit the difference between an observation and its possible cause.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a working kit and then open the switch. Ask what could make a similar bulb stay dark.
Suggest a break in the path and name a place to check.
Main activity · 30 min
Present one fault at a time. Ask for a prediction and a check before making a change. Open the switch before handling leads or the bulb.
Inspect each setup, propose a cause and observe whether correcting that single fault lights the bulb.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give a case with a loose lead and a case with a bulb shown loose in its holder. Ask for a cause and a suitable check in each.
Independently name both likely causes and describe checking the lead connection or reseating the bulb while the switch is open.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why pupils should check one possible fault at a time.
Explain how a single change helps identify which part caused the result.

lessons.title: Record What Happens When Objects Replace a Switch
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 81–83 · Activity Book p. 51
lessons.objective: Test four dry objects in the switch position and record whether the bulb lights for each object.
lessons.materials: Teacher-checked dry-cell test circuit with bulb and clip leads, uncoated steel washer, metal paper clip, rubber eraser, plastic lid and results table.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils recorded the results of all four trials. Recheck clip contact and the working kit with pupils whose records were incomplete.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show the bulb lighting with a closed switch. Ask what might happen if another object bridges the switch position.
Predict whether a selected object will let the bulb light.
Main activity · 30 min
Verify the kit with a known metal sample. Keep the bulb in the circuit and show how to clip each sample into the switch position. Use the same kit for all four objects.
Test the objects one at a time, observe the bulb and record each result as lights or does not light.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask each pupil to show their four-row table and repeat one trial if their observation differs from the group. Check the object names and observations.
Independently complete the table and explain which observation belongs to the repeated trial.
Closure · 5 min
Ask which part of the setup changed between trials.
Identify the sample as the changed object and name one part kept the same.

lessons.title: Classify Conductors and Insulators
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 81–83 · Activity Book pp. 52–53
lessons.objective: Classify four tested objects from their bulb results and state a rule linking each group to the flow of electric current.
lessons.materials: Recorded trials from the previous lesson, evidence cards, dry-cell test kit and a two-column classification sheet.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils classified all four objects and explained both groups. Revisit the trial evidence with pupils who sorted by appearance alone.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show two records with opposite bulb results. Ask what difference can be observed.
Identify which sample lit the bulb and which did not.
Main activity · 30 min
Build a class rule from the trial records. Demonstrate checking the tester and clip contact if an unexpected result occurs.
Group the samples by result and explain which group allowed current through the working test circuit.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Provide checked results for an aluminium tab, steel washer, rubber strip and plastic spoon. Ask each pupil to classify them and explain both groups.
Independently put the two metals under conductors and the rubber and plastic under insulators. State how current flow explains both results.
Closure · 5 min
Ask how to decide which group an unfamiliar object belongs to.
Explain how to test it in the working dry-cell circuit and use the bulb result.

lessons.title: Explain Observations From a Buzzer Circuit
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 76, 81–83 · Activity Book p. 54
lessons.objective: Communicate the buzzer's behaviour in two switch states and explain the sound using the condition of the circuit.
lessons.materials: Teacher-checked low-voltage buzzer matched to the classroom dry-cell kit, switch, insulated leads and individual sketch slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils explained both observations using the condition of the circuit. Repeat the demonstration with pupils who described the sound without explaining the path.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Demonstrate a buzzer briefly in the same type of circuit that previously used a bulb. Ask what pupils can observe.
Identify sound as the buzzer's observable output.
Main activity · 30 min
Let pairs trace the path through the buzzer and switch. Demonstrate both switch states and model recording the sound separately from its explanation.
Observe and record sound or silence in both states, then trace the path that accounts for each result.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask each pupil to present two observation–explanation pairs using a sketch, short caption or oral response. Check both switch states and the role of the buzzer.
Independently explain that the buzzer sounds when the circuit is complete and stops when the switch breaks the path.
Closure · 5 min
Ask which component controls whether the buzzer sounds in this setup.
Identify the switch and describe how it changes the path.

lessons.title: Describe Ways to Separate Mixtures
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 87–94 · Activity Book p. 55
lessons.objective: Name and describe a suitable method for at least four of five pictured mixtures.
lessons.materials: Trays, large coloured counters, dry sand and pebbles, sieve, large steel washers, wand magnet, cork, glass marbles, chalk in water and filter paper.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils described at least four suitable methods. Repeat a demonstration where pupils confused what passed through the tool with what stayed behind.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show two colours of counters in one tray and ask how they could be sorted.
Suggest a method and demonstrate removing one colour.
Main activity · 30 min
Set up examples of hand-picking, sieving, magnetic attraction, flotation and filtration. Demonstrate what each method removes or retains.
Visit the stations, match methods to mixtures and describe where each separated material ends up.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give picture cards showing mixed buttons, sand and pebbles, steel and plastic pieces, cork and stones in water, and fine chalk particles in water. Ask for a method and an action for each.
Independently name the five methods and describe at least four correctly, such as passing fine sand through the sieve while retaining the pebbles.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what pupils can see after the sand passes through the sieve.
Identify the sand below the sieve and the pebbles remaining above it.

lessons.title: Explain Why a Separation Method Works
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 89–94 · Activity Book pp. 56–57
lessons.objective: Choose suitable methods for three mixtures and explain each choice using a difference between the materials.
lessons.materials: Sand and pebbles, large steel washers and plastic counters, cork and glass marbles, a sieve, wand magnet, water tray and picture slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils linked all three choices to the relevant properties. Revisit the station with pupils who named a tool without explaining the material difference.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Hold up a sieve and a magnet beside a mixture of sand and pebbles. Ask which tool is useful here and why.
Choose the sieve and point to the difference in particle size.
Main activity · 30 min
Compare size, magnetic attraction and floating behaviour using the three mixtures. Model explaining a result by linking the property to what the tool does.
Select a tool or method, test it and discuss which difference helped separate the materials.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give fresh pictures of grit mixed with large beads, steel clips mixed with plastic pieces, and cork mixed with stones in water. Ask pupils to explain each choice.
Independently select sieving, magnetic attraction and flotation. Explain the size difference, attraction of steel and contrast between floating and sinking.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why a magnet did not help with cork and stones.
Explain that the chosen materials do not respond to the classroom magnet and recall the property that did help.

lessons.title: Investigate Which Materials Dissolve in Water
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 94–96 · Activity Book p. 58
lessons.objective: Record observations for four materials and classify all four as dissolving or remaining visible under the test conditions.
lessons.materials: Four labelled clear cups, equal water portions, small measured amounts of sugar, salt, sand and rice, separate stirrers and a results table.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils used all four observations to classify the samples. Repeat the check for settled particles with pupils who treated them as dissolved.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show salt before and after it dissolves in a glass. Ask whether the salt is still present.
Describe what can be seen and suggest that the salt is mixed into the water.
Main activity · 30 min
Use equal volumes, small portions of each material, equal stirring and the same observation time. Check that pupils record particles that settle as still visible.
Test each sample, note whether particles remain, and compare results with a partner.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask each pupil for an observation and classification in each row. Check that sugar and salt have dissolved and that sand and rice remain visible in the prepared test.
Independently record four observations, then use them to group sugar and salt together and sand and rice together.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what happened to the salt when it could no longer be seen.
Explain that it dissolved and remained mixed in the water.

lessons.title: Investigate the Effect of Water Temperature
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 96–97 · Activity Book p. 59 (temperature comparison)
lessons.objective: Compare dissolving times for equal sugar samples in cool and warm water and draw a conclusion supported by both results.
lessons.materials: Clear cups, cool water and teacher-prepared comfortably warm water, equal masses of the same sugar, identical stirrers, timer and record slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils drew a conclusion supported by both readings. Repeat the timing demonstration with pupils who confused a shorter time with slower dissolving.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show the two cups and ask which condition might make the same sugar dissolve sooner.
Predict the result and identify the temperature difference.
Main activity · 30 min
Keep water volume, sugar mass, grain size and stirring the same. Start both trials together and model timing until no grains remain visible.
Observe both cups, record each time and compare the readings.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask pupils to write both times, circle the shorter one and make a conclusion about temperature. Check the conclusion against the trial records.
Independently report both readings and say which condition dissolved the sugar sooner in the trial.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why using more sugar in one cup would affect the comparison.
Explain that both cups need the same amount so that temperature is the difference being tested.

lessons.title: Investigate the Effect of Stirring
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 97–98 · Activity Book p. 61
lessons.objective: Compare stirred and unstirred samples and support a conclusion with observations from both cups at the same time.
lessons.materials: Two clear cups, equal portions of water and table salt, stirrer, timer and a two-column observation slip.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils used observations from both cups to explain the effect of stirring. Review how to compare evidence from the same time point.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a spoon beside a cup with salt at the bottom. Ask how to check whether stirring makes a difference.
Suggest comparing one stirred cup with a second cup left still.
Main activity · 30 min
Keep water temperature, volume and salt mass the same. Ask groups to stir one cup steadily and observe both cups at agreed intervals.
Record the visible grains in each cup at the same times and compare what remains.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask pupils to record both observations at a time when the cups differ and explain which sample dissolved faster. Repeat the demonstration if the first trial gives no clear comparison.
Independently cite what remained visible in each cup and draw a conclusion about stirring.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why the group observed both cups at the same times.
Explain that a comparison needs observations from the same stage of the test.

lessons.title: Investigate the Effect of Particle Size
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 98–99 · Activity Book p. 60
lessons.objective: Compare the time for equal masses of fine and coarse sugar to dissolve and explain the result using the recorded times.
lessons.materials: Equal masses of sugar prepared from two identical cubes, one crushed finer than the other, clear cups, water, stirrers, timer and a record sheet.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils compared both times and identified a controlled factor. Repeat the equal-mass setup with pupils who used different amounts.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Display the two sugar portions and ask what is different and what has stayed the same.
Identify the different particle sizes and confirm that the portions have the same mass.
Main activity · 30 min
Keep water volume and temperature fixed. Have both pupils stir at the same pace and start timing together. Check that they use the same endpoint.
Time each sample until the grains are no longer visible and record both results.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask each pupil to report the two times, choose the faster sample and identify one factor kept the same.
Independently make the comparison and explain that the finer sugar dissolved sooner when the measurements support it.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what the test would show if the finer sample also used much warmer water.
Explain that the effects of temperature and particle size would be mixed.

lessons.title: Explain Observations About Mixtures
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 96–100 · Activity Book p. 62
lessons.objective: Communicate two observations about mixtures and give an evidence-based explanation for each using a sketch, caption or oral response.
lessons.materials: Class records from a sieving trial and the stirring investigation, a sample sketch and individual response slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils explained both observations using evidence. Revisit the class records with pupils who gave a conclusion without a matching observation.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a sieve with pebbles and a tray of sand underneath. Ask for one observation and then a reason.
Describe where each material ended up and suggest why.
Main activity · 30 min
Review the sieve and a paired stirred–unstirred record. Model labelling the evidence before explaining each result.
Discuss which evidence supports each explanation and practise showing it in a labelled sketch or sentence.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask pupils to explain the separation of sand and pebbles and one recorded effect of stirring. Check that each explanation refers to what was observed.
Independently communicate both observations and explain them using the sieve openings or the two dissolving results.
Closure · 5 min
Ask pupils to point to one part of a response that gives evidence.
Identify a detail that supports their explanation.

lessons.title: Identify Natural Sources of Water
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 101–104 · Activity Book pp. 63–64 (identify natural sources)
lessons.objective: Name five natural sources of water and match at least four to pictures that show their distinctive features.
lessons.materials: Illustrated cards for rain, river, lake, sea and spring, labels and individual response slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils named all five sources and made at least four correct matches. Compare two new pictures with pupils who confused a river with a spring.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show rain falling beside a photograph of a lake. Ask how the water appears in each picture.
Describe drops falling and water collected in a place surrounded by land.
Main activity · 30 min
Use a picture of water emerging from the ground to introduce a spring. Compare a river, lake and sea using visible features and model a five-branch map.
Sort pictures, name each water source and explain one visual clue to a partner.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give five new pictures, including a diagram of groundwater emerging at the surface. Check all five names and the links to the pictures.
Independently name rain, river, lake, sea and spring, then match the labels to the five pictures.
Closure · 5 min
Ask pupils to distinguish a spring from rain using their origin.
Explain that spring water comes out of the ground and rain falls from clouds.

lessons.title: Observe the Direction of Water Flow
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 105–106 · Activity Book p. 65
lessons.objective: Observe water in two tilted setups, mark the direction of flow in each and state how the direction relates to height.
lessons.materials: Shallow trays, small cups of coloured water, stable blocks, cloths and two-diagram response slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils drew both arrows correctly and supported the high-to-low rule. Repeat the reverse tilt with pupils who followed a fixed left-to-right direction.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a tray raised at one end. Ask where a small amount of water is likely to collect.
Point to a predicted end and explain the choice using height.
Main activity · 30 min
Guide groups to release water near the high end, record what happens and then reverse which end is raised.
Observe and sketch the flow in both setups. Compare where the water collects each time.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give two tray diagrams with opposite slopes. Ask pupils to mark arrows and support their rule with a trial observation.
Independently draw both arrows towards the lower ends and explain that the water changed direction when the high end changed.
Closure · 5 min
Ask whether water always flows to the right in this investigation.
Refer to the two trials and state that the direction depends on which end is lower.

lessons.title: Explain How Rivers and Waterfalls Flow
lessons.references: Textbook p. 107 · Activity Book pp. 66–67
lessons.objective: Use two landscape representations to generalise that rivers and waterfalls flow from higher to lower places.
lessons.materials: Waterfall photograph, river landscape diagram with marked heights, two new sketch cards and pencils.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils explained the same high-to-low pattern in both examples. Revisit the height marks with pupils who followed the layout of the page.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a waterfall photograph and ask where the water starts and lands.
Identify the top and the pool below and point to the direction of movement.
Main activity · 30 min
Compare the photograph with a river diagram showing a hillside and a lowland. Turn the diagram so the downhill path points the opposite way on the page.
Trace the water in each representation and explain what stays the same when the diagram is turned.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Provide a new waterfall sketch and a river sketch with high and low points. Check both arrows and a sentence supported by the examples.
Independently draw both arrows from higher to lower ground and state the common direction of natural water flow.
Closure · 5 min
Ask which clue is more useful, the side of the page or the height of the land.
Choose the land height and justify it with one example.

lessons.title: Sequence the Natural Water Cycle
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 108–109 · Activity Book p. 68
lessons.objective: Place four water-cycle stages in sequence and draw the return arrow to show that the cycle continues.
lessons.materials: Cards for surface water, water vapour, clouds and rain, arrow cards and blank cycle mats.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils ordered the stages and showed the return path correctly. Use an arrow mat with pupils who stopped the cycle at rain.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a picture of a puddle becoming smaller on a sunny day. Ask what may happen to some of the water.
Suggest that some water changes to vapour and mixes with the air.
Main activity · 30 min
Model arranging surface water, water vapour, clouds and rain. Explain that vapour cools into tiny droplets that form clouds and that rain returns water to rivers and seas.
Arrange the cards, link them with arrows and tell a partner how the final stage leads back to the first.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Provide a shuffled four-stage set. Check the order and direction of each arrow, including the return from rain to surface water.
Independently order and label the four stages and complete the circular path.
Closure · 5 min
Ask whether the cycle has to start with the sea in every diagram.
Point to a different starting stage and trace the same order around the cycle.

lessons.title: Explain Observations About the Water Cycle
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 108–109 · Activity Book p. 69
lessons.objective: Describe where droplets form and where they fall in a model, then link those observations to clouds and rain in the water cycle.
lessons.materials: Teacher-prepared clear bowl with comfortably warm water, clear cover cooled on top with an ice pack, response sheets.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils communicated both observations and linked them to the cycle. Compare the underside and top of the cover with pupils who attributed the droplets to the ice pack leaking.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a dry clear cover and ask pupils to predict where water might appear when it covers the bowl.
Make a prediction and identify the surface they will observe.
Main activity · 30 min
Keep the ice pack outside the covered bowl and point out droplets forming underneath. Observe droplets gathering and falling, then discuss how the cooled cover represents cooling in the air.
Record where droplets first appeared and where they moved. Explain how the model represents cloud droplets and rain.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask for a labelled sketch, short caption or oral response giving both observations and their links to the natural cycle.
Independently explain that vapour cooled into droplets on the underside and that larger drops fell, like rain returning water to the surface.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why the class used a dry cover at the start.
Explain that it helps establish that the droplets formed during the demonstration.

lessons.title: Show That Air Is Around Us
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 110–111 · Activity Book p. 70
lessons.objective: State that air surrounds us and describe two observations that show air can occupy space in familiar places.
lessons.materials: Clear cups, water basin, dry tissue, small clear bag and observation slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils stated that air surrounds us and described both observations. Repeat the two cup positions with pupils who thought the cup held nothing.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Hold up a limp clear bag, sweep it through the room and close it. Ask what made it expand.
Observe the change and suggest that air entered the bag.
Main activity · 30 min
Put tissue in the top of an inverted cup and lower it straight into water. Tilt the cup in a second trial so bubbles escape and water enters.
Compare both trials, observe the bubbles and describe how the air affected the water entering the cup.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask each pupil to state where the air came from in the bag and what the cup experiment showed. Check both explanations against the observations.
Independently state that air is around us, then explain that it filled the bag and occupied space in the inverted cup.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what the bubbles showed when the cup was tilted.
Explain that some air left the cup and moved through the water.

lessons.title: Name Gases Found in Air
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 110–111 · Activity Book p. 71
lessons.objective: State that air is a mixture of gases, name oxygen and carbon dioxide, and identify oxygen as a gas people need for breathing.
lessons.materials: Air-mixture diagram, gas word cards, breathing illustration and individual response slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils named both gases, explained that air is a mixture and identified oxygen for breathing. Revisit the labelled diagram with pupils who treated air and oxygen as the same thing.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a picture of a child breathing outdoors. Ask whether air is made of one gas or several.
Share a prediction and name any gas they already know.
Main activity · 30 min
Use a diagram that labels oxygen and carbon dioxide alongside other gases. Explain that oxygen is needed for breathing and that the air we breathe out still contains several gases.
Place the two gas labels in the air diagram and explain why the names do not describe all of the air.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask pupils to complete a short air-mixture statement, name two example gases and identify the gas people need for breathing.
Independently name oxygen and carbon dioxide, state that air contains several gases and select oxygen for breathing.
Closure · 5 min
Ask whether a bag filled with ordinary air contains only oxygen.
Explain that oxygen is one of several gases in the bag.

lessons.title: Describe Moving Air as Wind
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 112–113 · Activity Book p. 73
lessons.objective: Identify wind as moving air and give two observable signs that air moved during a classroom demonstration.
lessons.materials: Card fans, paper streamers, stands and individual comparison slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils defined wind and gave both signs of moving air. Repeat the still and moving conditions with pupils who named only the fan.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a hanging streamer before and after waving a card fan. Ask what changed without touching the streamer.
Describe the movement and suggest what reached the paper.
Main activity · 30 min
Guide pupils to alternate between holding the fan still and waving it from a marked distance. Ask them to notice both the streamer and the air they feel on a hand.
Compare the two conditions and record whether the paper moved and whether they felt air moving.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask each pupil to describe both signs and state what wind means. Check the link between the moving air and each observation.
Independently state that wind is moving air, then explain that they felt it and saw it move the streamer.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what pupils observed when the fan was held still.
Explain that the streamer stopped moving after the airflow from the fan stopped.

lessons.title: Explain How Wind Affects Daily Life
lessons.references: Textbook pp. 112–113, 115–116 · Activity Book pp. 74–75
lessons.objective: Give two useful effects of wind and one harmful effect of strong wind, explaining what changes in each case.
lessons.materials: Pictures of laundry, a sailing boat, a spinning windmill and strong wind near trees, with individual scenario cards.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils gave two useful effects and one harmful effect with clear explanations. Use pictures to help pupils link each effect to the object that changes.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show clothes on a line and ask how a breeze can affect them.
Suggest an effect and point to a clue in the picture.
Main activity · 30 min
Compare a helpful breeze with strong winds in several settings. Model a sentence linking moving air to a visible change.
Sort situations by effect and explain how air can move a sail or help dry laundry, and how strong wind can damage property.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give pictures of a sailboat, damp cloth and trees beside a roof during strong wind. Check two useful effects and one harmful effect with a reason for each.
Independently explain that wind pushes the sail, can help cloth dry faster and can cause branches or loose items to damage the roof.
Closure · 5 min
Ask how the same moving air can be useful in one situation and harmful in another.
