Ask pupils to name another short object and another longer distance.
Give a plausible example for each unit.

lessons.title: Measure Length and Draw Lines
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 56–58 · Activity Book pp. 126–127
lessons.objective: Measure a card strip to the nearest centimetre, mark a distance of 1 m and draw a straight line of a specified length.
lessons.materials: Centimetre rulers, measuring tapes, teacher-prepared 9 cm strips, masking tape and blank response slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils measured, marked and drew accurately. Repeat zero alignment with pupils whose answer was one graduation too large.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a strip whose end is aligned with the ruler's 1 cm mark. Ask what must be changed before reading the other end.
Move the first end to the zero mark and explain the starting position.
Main activity · 30 min
Model measuring a strip with both ends aligned to the scale and drawing a 6 cm line using marked endpoints. Show how to keep a measuring tape straight along a floor lane.
Measure two strips, draw a 6 cm line and take turns marking a 1 m distance with tape. Check a partner's zero and endpoint.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Provide a 9 cm strip and a new starting dot. Ask pupils to measure the strip, draw a 7 cm line and demonstrate the endpoint of 1 m at the station.
Independently record 9 cm, draw a 7 cm line from the dot and indicate the correct point on the floor lane.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why the ruler must stay still while a line is drawn.
Explain how a moving ruler can change the position or length of the line.

lessons.title: Estimate and Check Length
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 59–60 · Activity Book p. 128
lessons.objective: Use a benchmark to estimate two lengths, then measure them and state whether each estimate is shorter, longer or equal.
lessons.materials: A 10 cm benchmark strip, metre ruler, a classroom object suitable for cm, a distance suitable for m and recording tables.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils completed both estimate–measure comparisons with the correct units. Guide pupils who changed their original estimates to record both values separately.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show the 10 cm benchmark next to a longer strip. Ask whether the strip is closer to 10 cm or twice that length.
Use the benchmark to give and justify a rough estimate.
Main activity · 30 min
Model recording an estimate before measuring. Set up a short-object station and a longer-distance station with clear endpoints.
Choose cm or m, use the appropriate benchmark and record their estimates. Measure with a ruler or tape and compare with the estimates.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give each pupil two new lengths and ask for the estimate, actual reading and comparison for each. Check the measured values against the classroom setup.
Independently record both comparisons with units and describe one benchmark used.
Closure · 5 min
Ask how the 10 cm strip could help estimate an object's length without measuring it exactly.
Explain how to compare the object with the known length mentally.

lessons.title: Recognise Grams and Kilograms
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 61–62 · Activity Book p. 129
lessons.objective: Read a labelled scale in grams and a labelled scale in kilograms and select a suitable unit for two pictured objects.
lessons.materials: Gram and kilogram scales or dial models, labelled packets, a small eraser, a bag of books and response cards.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils read the two scales and chose both suitable units. Revisit the scale labels with pupils who wrote g and kg interchangeably.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a small eraser and a bag of books. Ask which would usually be described in grams.
Compare the objects and give a reason for their choice.
Main activity · 30 min
Show a gram scale and a kilogram scale. Compare the printed symbols and model reading the numbered graduation before saying the unit.
Match g to grams and kg to kilograms, then read labelled dial cards and match them to suitable examples.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Show dial readings at 300 on a g scale and 4 on a kg scale. Ask for suitable units for an eraser and a full schoolbag.
Independently write 300 g and 4 kg, then choose g for the eraser and kg for the schoolbag.
Closure · 5 min
Ask how to tell whether a displayed 4 is in grams or kilograms.
Point to the printed symbol on the scale.

lessons.title: Weigh Objects
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 p. 63 · Activity Book p. 130
lessons.objective: Check that a scale starts at zero, weigh two objects and record their readings with suitable units.
lessons.materials: Stable scales with appropriate capacity and clearly marked graduations, a small beanbag, a bag of books and a mass table.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils checked zero and recorded two valid readings. Revisit the meaning of each graduation with pupils whose units were correct but readings differed.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show the pointer on an empty scale. Ask what must be checked before adding an object.
Check that the pointer is on zero and suggest resetting it if needed.
Main activity · 30 min
Model placing an object on the centre of a scale and waiting for the reading to settle. Show how to count graduations when numbers are spaced apart.
Choose a suitable scale, take turns weighing a light object and a heavier one, then compare readings with a partner.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give pupils an individual turn at both stations. Check zero, the reading and the written unit against the measured classroom values.
Independently weigh both objects and record the readings in g or kg as displayed.
Closure · 5 min
Show a large empty container and a small solid object. Ask whether size alone determines mass.
Explain that both must be weighed to compare their mass reliably.

lessons.title: Estimate and Check Mass
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 64–65 · Activity Book p. 131
lessons.objective: Estimate two masses using a reference object, check both estimates on scales and describe the difference for each.
lessons.materials: A labelled 100 g reference and 1 kg reference, two suitable test objects, gram and kilogram scales, and a recording table.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils made two estimates and compared each with an actual reading. Revisit choosing a benchmark with pupils whose estimates used an unsuitable unit.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Let pupils compare a test object with the 100 g reference in their hands. Ask whether it feels lighter, heavier or similar.
Give a rough comparison using the known mass.
Main activity · 30 min
Model writing an estimate before weighing. Guide pupils to choose a reference near the expected mass and use a scale with suitable capacity.
Compare each object with a reference, estimate its mass with a unit and weigh it to obtain an actual reading.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Present two fresh objects, one for each scale. Check that each pupil records the estimate, reading and direction of the difference.
Independently compare their estimates with the measured masses and explain one estimate using the chosen reference.
Closure · 5 min
Ask which reference would be more useful for estimating a bag of books.
Choose the 1 kg reference and explain why it is closer in mass.

lessons.title: Recognise Millilitres and Litres
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 66–67 · Activity Book p. 132
lessons.objective: Read a marked graduation in millilitres and one in litres and match each unit to a plausible everyday quantity.
lessons.materials: Small graduated cylinder, large marked jug, bottle and carton labels, and picture slips with clear graduations.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils read both graduations and chose both units. Revisit the symbols with pupils who treated the quantities as interchangeable.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a small juice carton and a large water bottle. Ask pupils to find the quantity on each label.
Point to each quantity and notice that the labels use different units.
Main activity · 30 min
Show the graduations and symbols mℓ and ℓ on two containers. Model reading a marked line by saying both the value and the unit.
Match unit names to symbols and use picture cards to read labelled graduations and match them to everyday amounts.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Show marks at 250 on an mℓ scale and 2 on an ℓ scale. Ask for the likely units for a small juice carton and a large water container.
Independently record 250 mℓ and 2 ℓ, then select the suitable units for both objects.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what information the number 250 is missing when written on its own.
Name the unit needed to communicate the amount.

lessons.title: Measure Liquid Volume
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 68–69 · Activity Book p. 133
lessons.objective: Measure and record 150 mℓ and 1 ℓ using suitable vessels and read both levels at eye height.
lessons.materials: Water, a graduated plastic jug with a 150 mℓ mark, a larger jug with a 1 ℓ mark, trays and recording slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils measured both volumes and recorded them with suitable units. Reteach level placement and eye height for pupils who read from above.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show how a water level appears from above and from eye height. Ask which position gives a dependable reading.
Compare both views and choose eye height.
Main activity · 30 min
Place the vessel on a level surface and show how to add water slowly near the required mark. Use small and large vessels for the respective volumes.
Select a suitable vessel, pour water to a set level, wait for it to settle and read the scale at eye height.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask pupils to demonstrate 150 mℓ and 1 ℓ and check the vessel, reading position, level and written units.
Independently measure the two volumes and record each reading with its unit.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why a small cylinder is a poor choice for measuring a whole litre in one pour.
Explain that it lacks enough capacity.

lessons.title: Estimate and Check Liquid Volume
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 70–71 · Activity Book p. 134
lessons.objective: Use benchmarks to estimate two liquid volumes, measure both and compare each estimate with the actual reading.
lessons.materials: Clear benchmark vessels marked at 250 mℓ and 1 ℓ, two different containers with teacher-prepared water amounts, graduated jugs, trays and recording cards.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils estimated, measured and compared both volumes. Guide pupils who chose the taller vessel automatically to test equal volumes in two different shapes.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a narrow container and a wide container. Ask whether the taller water level always indicates more liquid.
Make a prediction and suggest measuring to check it.
Main activity · 30 min
Show a known 250 mℓ amount and a 1 ℓ amount. Model choosing the nearer reference before estimating and pouring into a measuring vessel to check.
Estimate the contents of the two containers, then pour and read the measuring scale. Record estimates and readings in separate columns.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Provide two new prepared amounts in different vessels. Check each estimate, measured value, unit and comparison without requiring exact predictions.
Independently estimate and measure both quantities and state whether each estimate was lower, higher or equal.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why a known reference helps when the containers have different shapes.
Explain that liquid height alone gives an incomplete comparison.

lessons.title: Solve Everyday Measurement Problems
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 72–75 · Activity Book pp. 135–136
lessons.objective: Solve three everyday problems covering length, mass and liquid volume and justify each answer with a comparison or calculation in the given unit.
lessons.materials: Height and clearance cards, mass cards, capacity pictures and individual response slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils solved all three problems and explained each decision in the given unit. Revisit identifying the quantity and the question with pupils who compared the wrong values.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a 90 cm shelf opening and a box that is 80 cm high. Ask how to decide whether the box fits.
Compare 80 cm with 90 cm and explain that the box fits with room to spare.
Main activity · 30 min
Model finding the known quantity and the requested decision in a shopping or classroom story. Compare capacities using the same units and ask pupils to show which quantity is bigger.
Mark the quantities, choose a comparison or calculation and explain the result using a sketch or number sentence.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give three cases: a 105 cm stand in a 100 cm space, a 350 g pack and a 500 g pack asking for the difference, and 600 mℓ of water with a 500 mℓ jug or a 750 mℓ jug.
Independently state that the stand is 5 cm too tall, calculate a 150 g difference and choose the 750 mℓ jug because it can hold 600 mℓ.
Closure · 5 min
Ask pupils to show which fact helped them choose the jug.
Point to the capacity and compare it with the amount to be poured.

lessons.title: Identify 3-D Shapes From Their Properties
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 77–79 · Activity Book p. 139
lessons.objective: Identify at least four of five solids from property clues and justify one choice using a face, surface or vertex.
lessons.materials: Cube, non-cube cuboid, square-based pyramid, cylinder and cone models, property cards and five individual clues.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils identified at least four solids and justified one match. Let pupils who confused two solids compare their models side by side.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a cube and a cylinder. Ask what can be noticed by placing each on its side.
Describe a visible difference and point to a flat or curved surface.
Main activity · 30 min
Model tracing a face and pointing to a vertex on a solid. Give pairs descriptions of the five solids, using distinguishing properties for each.
Turn and inspect the models, match them to the clues and explain which property separates similar choices.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give clues for six equal square faces, a rectangular box with unequal dimensions, a square base with four triangular faces, two circular flat faces, and one circular base with a point.
Independently identify the cube, cuboid, square-based pyramid, cylinder and cone respectively. Justify one match using a named property.
Closure · 5 min
Ask how to distinguish the cone from the cylinder using their flat faces.
State that the cone has one circular flat face and the cylinder has two.

lessons.title: Identify the Basic Shapes of 3-D Solids
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 p. 80 · Activity Book p. 140
lessons.objective: Name the basic shapes and state their counts for at least two of three solids, including one with a curved surface.
lessons.materials: Foldable solids, circular lids, detachable cylinder wrap, detachable cone wrap, and shape-and-count cards.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils identified at least two complete sets of pieces, including one curved solid. Reopen a model with pupils who counted only the visible parts.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Press a flat cube face onto paper and trace its outline. Ask what 2-D shape appears.
Identify the square and point to a second square face.
Main activity · 30 min
Trace the flat bases of a cylinder and cone. Unwrap the side surfaces to show a rectangle for the cylinder and a sector for the cone.
Trace or unfold models, then record which flat pieces and how many of each make up the solid.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give pictures of a square-based pyramid, cylinder and cone. Ask for the names and counts of the pieces that form each one.
Independently record one square and four triangles, two circles and one rectangle, and one circle and one sector, respectively.
Closure · 5 min
Ask which two models use circles and how many each uses.
Compare the single circle of the cone with the two of the cylinder.

lessons.title: Recognise Nets of 3-D Shapes
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 81–83 · Activity Book pp. 141–142
lessons.objective: Match at least four of five nets to their solids and identify two different arrangements that fold into cubes.
lessons.materials: Five pre-cut nets with tabs where appropriate, solid models, two valid cube nets and a strip of six squares as a comparison.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils matched at least four nets and identified both cube nets. Let pupils who chose the strip trace where the faces would overlap or fail to close.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Open a small cube carton along prepared edges and lay it flat. Ask what remained the same.
Compare the closed carton and the net, noting the same six square faces.
Main activity · 30 min
Supply nets for a cube, cuboid, square-based pyramid, cylinder and cone. Ask pupils to predict and fold before matching. Show how a strip of six squares fails to close as a cube.
Fold models, match each net to a solid and compare two working cube arrangements with the strip.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give five net cards for matching. Then offer three cube candidates and ask pupils to select the two that close without overlapping.
Independently match the five cards and mark the two working cube nets, using a fold or a sketch to check.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why counting six squares alone does not prove a cube net will work.
Explain that the squares also need an arrangement that closes into six different faces.

lessons.title: Identify 2-D Shapes From Their Properties
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 84–85 · Activity Book p. 143
lessons.objective: Identify a square, a non-square rectangle, a triangle and a circle from descriptions and justify one match.
lessons.materials: Flat shape cards in varied sizes and orientations, rulers, everyday object pictures and clue slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils identified all four shapes and justified one match. Revisit any rotated example that was identified by its position rather than its properties.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Rotate a square card and ask whether the number and lengths of its sides changed.
Count the sides again and explain why the rotated card still represents a square.
Main activity · 30 min
Model reading descriptions about straight sides, corners, equal lengths and a curved boundary. Show a square alongside a rectangle with two long and two short sides.
Compare the shapes, sort the descriptions and explain how the side lengths distinguish the two cards.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give four property descriptions in a new order and ask for one written or oral reason.
Independently identify all four shapes and refer to a matching property for one of them.
Closure · 5 min
Ask which shape has no straight sides and no corners.
Identify the circle and trace its curved boundary.

lessons.title: Draw Basic 2-D Shapes
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 86–87 · Activity Book p. 144
lessons.objective: Draw and name a square, a non-square rectangle, a triangle and a circle using suitable tools.
lessons.materials: Grid paper, rulers, triangle dot cards, circular stencils and individual drawing sheets.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils drew and labelled all four shapes. Practise using grid intersections or a stencil with pupils who left gaps or changed a required side length.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Draw three connected lines with a gap and ask what is needed to make a closed triangle.
Point to the gap and suggest connecting the final corners.
Main activity · 30 min
Model drawing a square and rectangle on a grid, joining three points with a ruler and tracing a circle. Show how to check corners and lengths before labelling.
Practise drawing each shape, compare a square with the non-square rectangle and use a partner's checklist to review the drawings.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Ask for a 3-by-3 square, a 5-by-2 rectangle, a triangle from three provided dots and a circle traced from a stencil.
Independently draw and label the four shapes. Check that every outline is closed.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what a pupil can check to tell the two four-sided drawings apart.
Compare the lengths of adjacent sides on the grid.

lessons.title: Solve Everyday Problems About Shapes
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 88–89 · Activity Book pp. 145–146
lessons.objective: Solve two everyday design problems and justify each selection with a matching property or set of net pieces.
lessons.materials: Reusable packaging models, pattern cards for solid nets, label templates and individual design slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils solved both cases and justified each choice. Revisit matching the words in each design brief to a shape property.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a round lid beside a square box opening. Ask whether the lid matches the opening.
Compare their outlines and explain the mismatch.
Main activity · 30 min
Model choosing a net for a square-based pyramid display using one square and four triangles. Ask pairs to justify a different package choice using its pieces.
Sketch a plan, match the net to a model and explain why a competing pattern would make another solid.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Give two problems: choose a net to make a round tin model with two flat ends, and choose a label with four equal straight sides to cover a square card.
Independently select the net with two matching circles and a rectangle and the square label. Give a reason for each selection.
Closure · 5 min
Ask which clue would distinguish a cone pattern from the tin pattern.
Name the one circle and sector of a cone and compare them with the tin's pieces.

lessons.title: Collect and Organise Everyday Data
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 91–93 · Activity Book pp. 149–150
lessons.objective: Collect one response from each pupil in a small group, record each response once and check that the category totals match the number of responses.
lessons.materials: Three activity picture cards, response tokens, tally sheets and an individual set of eight coded survey slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils recorded all categories and checked the total correctly. Practise moving each counted slip to a separate pile with pupils who counted a slip twice.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Ask which of three indoor activities the class would choose. Discuss how to give everyone one vote.
Suggest recording one choice for each pupil.
Main activity · 30 min
Model putting one tally in the correct category for each response and bundling every fifth mark. Assign a collector and checker in each group, then swap roles.
Collect responses, sort tokens into categories, tally the choices and check that the counts add up to the number surveyed.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Hand out eight anonymous survey slips with four drawing choices, three reading choices and one puzzle choice in mixed order. Check each tally and total.
Independently sort and tally the slips, write the three counts and check that 4 + 3 + 1 = 8.
Closure · 5 min
Ask what a total of nine would suggest if only eight slips were collected.
Explain that a response may have been counted twice or an extra mark may have been added.

lessons.title: Read a Vertical Bar Chart
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 94–96 · Activity Book p. 151 · Activity 1
lessons.objective: Identify the meaning of both axes, read three bar values and identify the highest and lowest categories on a vertical bar chart.
lessons.materials: Teacher-drawn vertical charts with one-unit marks, axis labels, rulers and individual answer slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils identified both axes, read all three values and found both extremes. Trace across from the bar top with pupils who read between adjacent ticks.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Display a chart titled Books Borrowed and ask what its title tells us before reading the bars.
Explain what is counted and locate the category names.
Main activity · 30 min
Show how to move from a category to the top of its bar and across to the number axis. Point out the zero and one-unit graduations.
Take turns tracing bar tops to the scale, stating values with their units and finding the highest and lowest bars.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Display a new chart showing four adventure books, seven animal books and two poetry books borrowed. Ask for both axes, all three values and the two extremes.
Independently name the category and number axes, record 4, 7 and 2, and identify animal books as highest and poetry books as lowest.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why the scale matters even if a bar looks tall.
Explain that its height must be read against the numbered marks to obtain a count.

lessons.title: Read a Horizontal Bar Chart
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 94–96 · Activity Book p. 152 · Activity 2
lessons.objective: Read four values from a horizontal bar chart, identify the largest category and calculate the total of the four values.
lessons.materials: Teacher-drawn horizontal charts with zero and one-unit graduations, category cards, rulers and answer slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils read all four values, named the largest category and found the total. Revisit the end of each bar with pupils who read the row position as a count.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Display a horizontal chart and ask which axis carries the numbers.
Point to the horizontal number axis and the vertical category axis.
Main activity · 30 min
Model following a bar to its right end and then down to the scale. Have pairs read a chart and check their values by tracing the same path.
Read values with category names, compare the bar lengths and add the counts when asked for the total.
Practice and assessment · 20 min
Show a chart of six bus riders, five walkers, two cyclists and four car riders. Ask for all counts, the largest category and the total.
Independently read 6, 5, 2 and 4, identify bus riders as the largest group and add the values to get 17 pupils.
Closure · 5 min
Ask whether the top row always has the highest count.
Explain that the longest bar indicates the highest count, whichever row it occupies.

lessons.title: Solve Everyday Problems With Data
lessons.references: Textbook Part 2 pp. 97–99 · Activity Book pp. 153–154
lessons.objective: Use a table or bar chart to answer a total, a difference and a decision question, giving a reason for the decision.
lessons.materials: Teacher-made charts with one-unit scales, a tally table, question cards and individual response slips.
lessons.reflection: ___ of ___ pupils answered all three questions and justified the decision using the data. Revisit marking only the relevant bars with pupils who used the wrong categories.
phases: Set induction · 5 min
Show a chart about lunchtime games and ask which bars could help choose a game for the class.
Identify the relevant bars and suggest comparing their counts.
Main activity · 30 min
Model finding relevant values in a tally table and a bar chart. Contrast a question asking how many altogether with one asking how many more.
Identify the needed categories, read their values and explain when to add or subtract.
Practice and assessment · 20 min

Give a chart with eight votes for chess, six for draughts and three for puzzles. Ask for the total, the difference between chess and puzzles, and which game to buy if the rule is to buy the most requested.
Independently give 17 votes, a difference of 5 votes and choose chess because its 8 votes exceed both other counts.
Closure · 5 min
Ask why the total vote count cannot identify the most requested game by itself.
Explain that the decision needs a comparison of the individual category counts.
